To show \(\lim_{x\to 0}g(x)=0\), let \(\varepsilon>0\).
If \(x\in\mathbb{Q}\), then \(g(x)=0\), so \(|g(x)-0|=0<\varepsilon\).
If \(x\notin\mathbb{Q}\), then \(g(x)=x\), so \(|g(x)-0|=|x|<\varepsilon\) whenever \(|x|<\varepsilon\).
Hence for \(\delta=\varepsilon\), Definition 2 gives \(\lim_{x\to0}g(x)=0\).
Now let \(x_0\neq0\). Take \(\varepsilon=|x_0|/2\). For any \(\delta>0\), set \(\delta_0=\min\{\delta,|x_0|/2\}\) and pick a rational \(q\) and an irrational \(r\) such that \(0<|q-x_0|<\delta_0\) and \(0<|r-x_0|<\delta_0\). Then \(g(q)=0\), while \(g(r)=r\). Since \[
|r| \geq ||x_0|-|r-x_0|| > \frac{|x_0|}{2}=\varepsilon,
\] there is no single \(L\) such that \(|g(r)-L|<\varepsilon\) together with \(|g(q)-L|<\varepsilon\). Thus \(\lim_{x\to x_0}g(x)\) does not exist for \(x_0\neq0\).

1 Introduction


2 Unbounded limits
The notion of limit considered here requires the actual limit to be a finite real number. However, there are situations in which the closer we get to a point in the domain, the more the function increases or decreases.
For instance, let \(D=\mathbb{R}-\{0\}\), and consider the function \(f\colon D\subset \rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x}\). We can compute \(f(x)\) for values of \(x\) which are closer and closer to \(0\). For positive values of \(x\), we see that the closer \(x\) is to \(0\), the bigger \(f(x)\) is. However, for negative values of \(x\), the closer \(x\) is to \(0\), the more \(f(x)\) becomes bigger in absolute value but with negative sign.
Faced with this situation, we conjecture that the limit at \(x_{0}^{\pm}\) does not exist in the sense of this definition. However, since we do have the intuitive understanding of how \(f\) behaves around \(0\) (it increases indefinitely when \(x\rightarrow 0^+\), and decreases indefinitely when \(x\rightarrow 0^{-}\)), we would like to be able to make this intuitive understanding rigorous. A suitable way to do it is by introducing the notion of unbounded limits.






NoteUnbounded limits




Definition 1 Consider the function \(f\colon D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\). If \(x_{0}\) is an accumulation point for \(D\), we say that the formal equality \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}} f(x)=+\infty
\] holds if for every \(K>0\) there is a \(0< \delta\) such that \[
x\in D,\quad 0<|x-x_{0}|<\delta \Longrightarrow f(x)>K.
\] In this case, we say that \(+\infty\) is the limit of \(f\) at \(x_{0}\).
Analogously, we say that the formal equality \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}} f(x)=-\infty
\] holds if for every \(K>0\) there is a \(0< \delta\) such that \[
x\in D,\quad 0<|x-x_{0}|<\delta \Longrightarrow f(x)< -K.
\] In this case, we say that \(-\infty\) is the limit of \(f\) at \(x_{0}\).
If \(x_{0}\) is a right accumulation point for \(D\), the right unbounded limits are defined by replacing \[
0<|x- x_{0}|<\delta
\] with \[
x\in D,\quad 0<x-x_{0}<\delta.
\] If \(x_{0}\) is a left accumulation point for \(D\), the left unbounded limits are defined by replacing \[
0<|x- x_{0}|<\delta
\] with \[
x\in D,\quad 0<x_{0}-x<\delta.
\]



Before proceeding further, we need to make sure that the idea of unbounded limits formalized in Definition 1 makes actual sense.
First of all, just as we did for regular limits here, we must ensure that the notions of unbounded limits and unbounded left and right limits are well-posed.






NoteWell-posedness of unbounded limits




Proposition 1 Let \(x_{0}\) be an accumulation point for \(D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\), and consider the function \(f\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\). If \[
\begin{split}
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}f(x)&=L \\
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}f(x)&=M,
\end{split}
\] according to Definition 1, with \(L,M\in\{+\infty,-\infty\}\), then \(L=M\).
Under the obvious modifications, a similar result holds for left and right unbounded limits.


Proof:

The proof is a slight modification of that given here, and you are strongly invited to try to fill the gaps on your own.




Then, similarly to what we did here, we have to check what is the relation between the existence of an unbounded limit at \(x_{0}\) and the existence of left and right unbounded limits at \(x_{0}\).






CautionExistence and equality of left and right unbounded limits at \(x_{0}\) is equivalent to existence of the unbounded limit at \(x_{0}\)




Exercise 1 Let \(x_{0}\) be an accumulation point for \(D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\), and consider the function \(f\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\). Show that the unbounded limit \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}f(x)=\pm \infty
\] holds if and only if if both left and right unbounded limits at \(x_{0}\) exist and are equal.


Solution:

You are strongly invited to try to solve it on your own.




Finally, we have to verify that different functions that agree on an arbitrary subset of the intersection of their domains have the same unbounded limits (when they exist) at the points of the intersection.






CautionUnbounded limits of the restriction




Exercise 2 Let \(D,D'\subseteq \mathbb{R}\) be such that \(D\cap D'\neq\emptyset\), and consider two functions \(f\colon D \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) and \(g\colon D'\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) such that \(g(x)=f(x)\) on \(S\subseteq D\cap D'\). If \(x_{0}\) is an accumulation point for \(S\) prove that \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}} f(x)=\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}} g(x)
\] whenever either one of the limits exist in accordance with Definition 1.
Prove analogous results for the case of left and right limits.


Solution:

You are strongly invited to try to solve it on your own following what you should have already done for this exercise.




Let us now apply Definition 1 to rigorously investigate what happens in the motivating example \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x}\) discussed above.






TipThe case \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x}\)




Example 1 Let \(f\colon \mathbb{R}-\{0\}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) be given by \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x}\). The point \(0\) is an accumulation point for the domain of \(f\), so it makes sense to investigate the limit for \(x\rightarrow 0\). As mentioned before, when \(x\) reaches \(0\) from the right, the function \(f\) increases, while it decreases when \(x\) reaches \(0\) from the left. Therefore, we conjecture that \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow 0^{\pm}} \frac{1}{x}=\pm\infty .
\] Let us consider \(x\rightarrow 0^{+}\), so that \(x>0\). Following Definition 1, we see that \[
x-0<\delta \implies \frac{1}{\delta}<\frac{1}{x}=f(x) .
\] Therefore, taking \(\frac{1}{\delta}> K\), our conjecture follows. The case \(x\rightarrow 0^{-}\) follows analogously.



The algebraic manipulations of limits here can be appropriately modified to handle also unbounded limits, provided the so-called inderminate forms are treated with care.






NoteAlgebraic manipulations of unbounded limits




Proposition 2 Let \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\), let \(x_{0}\) be an accumulation point for \(D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\), and consider two functions \(f,g\colon D\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\). If \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}f(x)=L_{1} \mbox{ and } \quad \lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}g(x)=L_{2}
\] in the sense of this definition or Definition 1, then \[
\begin{split}
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}} \left(\alpha \,f + \beta \,g \right)(x) &=\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}  \alpha \,f (x) + \lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}} \beta \, g(x) =  \alpha\,L_{1} + \beta \,L_{2} \\ & \\
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}} \left((\alpha \,f)\cdot(\beta \,g)\right) (x) & =\left(\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}} \alpha \,f(x)\right)\left(\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}  \beta \,g(x)\right)= \alpha\,L_{1}\,\beta \,L_{2}  \\ & \\
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}\,\left(\frac{\alpha \,f}{\beta \,g}\right)(x)&=\frac{\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0} }\alpha \,f(x)}{\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0} }\beta \,g(x)} =\frac{\alpha_{1}L_{1}}{\alpha_{2} L_{2}},
\end{split}
\] where \(\alpha_{2},L_{2}\neq 0\) is assumed in the last equality, and where the following “conventions” are enforced: \[
\begin{split}
1) & \quad  L + (\pm\infty) =\pm \infty \;\mbox{ if }\;\; L\in\mathbb{R} \mbox{ or } L=\pm\infty\\ & \\
2) & \quad L\cdot \pm\infty = \pm \infty  \;\mbox{ if }\;\; l>0\\ & \\
3) & \quad l\cdot \pm\infty = \mp \infty  \;\mbox{ if }\;\; l<0\\ & \\
4) & \quad \frac{L}{\pm\infty} = 0  \;\mbox{ if }\;\; L\neq  \pm \infty\\ & \\
5) & \quad \frac{\pm\infty}{l} = \pm \infty  \;\mbox{ if }\;\; l>0\\ & \\
6) & \quad \frac{\pm\infty}{l} = \mp \infty  \;\mbox{ if }\;\; l<0\\ & \\
7) & \quad \frac{l}{0} =+\infty \;\mbox{ if }\;\; \left\{\begin{matrix}l>0 \mbox{ and } g(x)>0 \\ \mbox{ or } \\ l<0 \mbox{ and } g(x)<0\end{matrix}\right.\\ & \\
8) & \quad \frac{l}{0} =-\infty \;\mbox{ if }\;\; l<0 .
\end{split}
\] All other cases are called indeterminate forms, and require a case by case analysis to determine if the limit on the left exists or not.
Under the obvious modifications, the same conclusions hold for left and right limits.


Proof:

The case where both limits are real numbers is already done here.
The rest of the proof is tedious, and it will likely take me some time to be uploaded.




Also the squeeze theorem can be adapted to unbounded limits.






NoteThe squeeze (pinching) theorem for unbounded limits




Theorem 1 Let \(x_{0}\) be an accumulation point of \(D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\), and consider the functions \(f,g\colon D\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\). If \(g(x)\leq f(x)\) for all \(x\in D\) and \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}g(x)= +\infty,
\] then it follows that \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}f(x)=+\infty.
\] Analogously, if \(f(x)\leq g(x)\) for all \(x\in D\) and \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}g(x)= -\infty,
\] then it follows that \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}f(x)=-\infty.
\]
Under the obvious modifications, the same conclusions hold for left and right limits.


Proof:

The proof is similar to that given here, but it will take me some time to upload it.




We can also adapt the proposition on the limit of composite functions to the case of unbounded limits.






NoteUnbounded limit of composite functions




Proposition 3 Consider \(D,D'\subseteq\mathbb{R}\), let \(x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(l\in\mathbb{R}\) be accumulation points for \(D'\) and \(D\), respectively, and take two functions \(f\colon D \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) and \(g\colon D' \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\). Suppose that \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}g(x) = l\in\mathbb{R},
\tag{1}\] and that \[
\qquad \lim_{y\rightarrow l} f(y) =\pm\infty.
\tag{2}\] Then, the equality \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}} f\circ g(x)=\pm\infty
\] holds if there is an open interval \(I\) centered at \(x_{0}\) on which \(g(x)\neq l\) for all \(x_{0}\neq x\in I\).
Under the obvious modifications, analogous results hold for left and right limits.


Proof:

The proof is essentially the same as that given here.
Let us consider only the case where the limit in Equation 2 is \(+\infty\), because the \(-\infty\) can be proved by analogy. From Equation 2, given \(K>0\), it follows that there is \(\eta>0\) for which \[
0<|y-l|<\eta \implies f(y)>K,
\tag{3}\] with \(y\neq l\). On the other hand, Equation 1 implies that, given the same \(\eta>0\) as before, there is \(\delta>0\) such that \[
0<|x-x_{0}|<\delta \implies  |g(x) - l|<\eta.
\tag{4}\] Setting \(y=g(x)\), the assumption on \(g\) implies we can take \(\delta>0\) such that \(0<|x-x_{0}|<\delta\) implies \(x\in I\) and thus \(g(x)\neq l\) by assumption. Consequently, it holds \[
0<|x-x_{0}|<\delta \implies  0<|g(x) - l|<\eta \implies |f(g(x)) -L|<\varepsilon,
\] as desired.






3 Limits at infinity
It should be quite easy to convince ourselves that the function \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \(f(x)=x + c\), with \(c\in\mathbb{R}\), is obliged to increase/decrease indefinitely as the input \(x\) increases/decreases indefinitely. It should be less easy, but still quite manageable without too much thought, to convince ourselves that the function \(g\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \(g(x)=x^{2}+c\), is obliged to increase indefinitely irrespectively of the input \(x\) increasing or decreasing indefinitely. We could dare to say that no sophisticated mathematical reasoning is necessary for us to confidently believe these ‘facts’.
However, a different situation is presented to us if we consider the function \(h\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \(h(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{x^{2}+1}\). We ‘know’ that both the numerator and the denominator of \(h\) grow indefinitely irrespectively of the input \(x\) increasing or decreasing, but it’s difficult to get a clear mental picture of what really happens when \(x\) increases/decreases indefinitely just by looking at the definition of the function. After some thinking, we may arrive to the conclusion that, since the numerator and denominator only differ by \(1\), their ratio gets increasingly close to \(1\). Some quick numerical checks with \(x=100,1000,10000,100000\) may support this intuition, but we can not be as sure as we were for the cases \(f(x)=x\) or \(g(x)=x^{2}+c\) mentioned before.
Then, we may start to wonder about more complex examples like \(t\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \(t(x)=\frac{x^{3}-3x^{2}}{x^{2}+x^{4}}\) or \(t(x)=\frac{\sqrt{x^{4}+3x^{2}}}{x^{2}+x^{4}+83}\), and we quickly realize we have no idea other than plugging in some numbers and hoping some pattern emerges to guide our intuition.
From a mathematician’s point of view, this is the appropriate moment to go looking for a new concept of limit that can help us understanding what happens when the input variable either grows or degrows indefinitely, by giving us rigorous analytical tools to guide our intuition. Luckily for us, this new notion of limit has been found quite some time, and we can ‘simply’ exploit its power.






NoteLimits at \(+\infty\)




Definition 2 Let \(D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\) be such that \(+\infty\) is a right accumulation point for it, and consider a function \(f\colon D\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\).
The formal equality \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow +\infty} f(x)= L
\] holds with \(L\in\mathbb{R}\) if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(\varrho>0\) such that \[
D\ni x> \varrho \Longrightarrow |f(x) - L|<\varepsilon .
\]
The formal equality \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow +\infty} f(x)=+\infty
\] holds if for every \(K>0\) there is \(\varrho>0\) such that \[
D\ni x> \varrho \Longrightarrow f(x)>K.
\]
The formal equality
\[
\lim_{x\rightarrow +\infty} f(x)=-\infty
\] holds if for every \(K>0\) there is \(\varrho>0\) such that \[
D\ni x> \varrho \Longrightarrow f(x)<-K.
\]









NoteLimits at \(-\infty\)




Definition 3 Let \(D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\) be such that \(-\infty\) is a left accumulation point for it, and consider a function \(f\colon D\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\).
The formal equality \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow -\infty} f(x)= L
\] holds with \(L\in\mathbb{R}\) if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(\varrho>0\) such that \[
D\ni x<-\varrho \Longrightarrow |f(x) - L|<\varepsilon .
\]
The formal equality \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow -\infty} f(x)=+\infty
\] holds if for every \(K>0\) there is \(\varrho>0\) such that \[
D\ni x<- \varrho \Longrightarrow f(x)>K.
\]
The formal equality
\[
\lim_{x\rightarrow -\infty} f(x)=-\infty
\] holds if for every \(K>0\) there is \(\varrho>0\) such that \[
D\ni x<- \varrho \Longrightarrow f(x)<-K.
\]



Once again, we need to check that the notions of limits at infinity introduced in Definition 2 and Definition 3 are well-posed. We start with the uniqueness of the limit at infinity.






NoteWell-posedness of limits at infinity




Proposition 4 Let \(+\infty\) be an accumulation point of \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\), and consider the function \(f\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\). If \[
\begin{split}
\lim_{x\rightarrow +\infty}f(x)&=L \\
\lim_{x\rightarrow +\infty}f(x)&=M,
\end{split}
\] according to Definition 2, then \(L=M\).
Under the obvious modifications, a similar result holds for \(x\rightarrow-\infty\).


Proof:

The proof is a slight modification of that given here, and you are strongly invited to fill the gaps on your own.




Then, we check that the notion of limits at infinity does not lead to weird situations when different functions agreeing on an arbitrary subset of the intersection of their domains are considered.






CautionLimits at infinity of the restriction




Exercise 3 Let \(D,D'\subseteq \mathbb{R}\) be such that \(D\cap D'\neq\emptyset\), and consider two functions \(f\colon D \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) and \(g\colon D'\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) such that \(g(x)=f(x)\) on \(S\subseteq D\cap D'\). If \(\pm\infty\) is an accumulation point for \(S\) prove that \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty} f(x)=\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty} g(x)
\] whenever either one of the limits exist in the sense of Definition 2 or Definition 3.


Solution:

You are strongly invited to try to solve it on your own following what you should have already done for this exercise and Exercise 2.




Let us now use Definition 2 and Definition 3 to disucss two simple but important examples.






TipBasic examples of limits at infinity




Example 2 Consider the function \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) given by \(f(x)=x\). We want to prove that \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow\pm\infty} x=\pm\infty.
\] Focusing on the case \(x\rightarrow +\infty\), Definition 2 requires us to prove that, given \(K>0\), there is \(M>0\) such that \[
x>M\implies x>K.
\] Taking \(M>K\) is enough.
For the case \(x\rightarrow -\infty\), Definition 3 requires us to prove that, given \(K>0\), there is \(M>0\) such that \[
x<-M\implies x<-K.
\] Taking (again) \(M>K\) is enough.

Consider the function \(f\colon D\subset \mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) given by \(f(x)=x\), where \(D\) is any subset not containing \(0\) and such that \(\pm\infty\) is an accumulation point. We want to prove that \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow\pm\infty} \frac{1}{x}=0.
\] \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow\pm\infty} x=\pm\infty.
\] Focusing on the case \(x\rightarrow +\infty\), Definition 2 requires us to prove that, given \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(M>0\) such that \[
x>M\implies |f(x) - 0|= \frac{1}{x}<\varepsilon.
\] Since \(x>M>0\) implies \(0<\frac{1}{x}<\frac{1}{M}\), taking \(M\) such that \(\frac{1}{M}<\varepsilon\) is enough.
For the case \(x\rightarrow -\infty\), Definition 3 requires us to prove that, given \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(M>0\) such that \[
x<-M<0\implies |f(x) - 0|= -\frac{1}{x}<\varepsilon.
\] Since \(x<-M<0\) implies \(0<-\frac{1}{x}<\frac{1}{M}\), taking (again) \(M\) such that \(\frac{1}{M}<\varepsilon\) is enough.



The algebraic manipulations of limits here can be appropriately modified to handle also limits at infinity, provided we handle the so-called inderminate forms with care.






NoteAlgebraic manipulations of improper limits




Proposition 5 Let \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\), let \(\pm\infty\) be an accumulation point for \(D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\), and consider two functions \(f,g\colon D\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\). If \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty}f(x)=L_{1} \mbox{ and } \quad \lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty}g(x)=L_{2}
\] in the sense of Definition 2 or Definition 3, then \[
\begin{split}
\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty} \left(\alpha \,f + \beta \,g \right)(x) &=\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty}  \alpha \,f (x) + \lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty} \beta \, g(x) =  \alpha\,L_{1} + \beta \,L_{2} \\ & \\
\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty} \left((\alpha \,f)\cdot(\beta \,g)\right) (x) & =\left(\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty} \alpha \,f(x)\right)\left(\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty}  \beta \,g(x)\right)= \alpha\,L_{1}\,\beta \,L_{2}  \\ & \\
\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty}\,\left(\frac{\alpha \,f}{\beta \,g}\right)(x)&=\frac{\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty }\alpha \,f(x)}{\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty }\beta \,g(x)} =\frac{\alpha_{1}L_{1}}{\alpha_{2} L_{2}},
\end{split}
\] where \(\alpha_{2},L_{2}\neq 0\) is assumed in the last equality, and where the following “conventions” are enforced: \[
\begin{split}
1) & \quad  L + (\pm\infty) =\pm \infty \;\mbox{ if }\;\; L\in\mathbb{R} \mbox{ or } L=\pm\infty\\ & \\
2) & \quad L\cdot \pm\infty = \pm \infty  \;\mbox{ if }\;\; l>0\\ & \\
3) & \quad l\cdot \pm\infty = \mp \infty  \;\mbox{ if }\;\; l<0\\ & \\
4) & \quad \frac{L}{\pm\infty} = 0  \;\mbox{ if }\;\; L\neq  \pm \infty\\ & \\
5) & \quad \frac{\pm\infty}{l} = \pm \infty  \;\mbox{ if }\;\; l>0\\ & \\
6) & \quad \frac{\pm\infty}{l} = \mp \infty  \;\mbox{ if }\;\; l<0\\ & \\
7) & \quad \frac{l}{0} =+\infty \;\mbox{ if }\;\; \left\{\begin{matrix}l>0 \mbox{ and } g(x)>0 \\ \mbox{ or } \\ l<0 \mbox{ and } g(x)<0\end{matrix}\right.\\ & \\
8) & \quad \frac{l}{0} =-\infty \;\mbox{ if }\;\; l<0 .
\end{split}
\] All other cases are called indeterminate forms, and require a case by case analysis to determine if the limit on the left exists or not.
Under the obvious modifications, the same conclusions hold for left and right limits.


Proof:

The proof is similar to the one already done here, and to the proof of Proposition 2. However, it will likely take me some time to upload it.




Now, we can go back and understand the ‘complex examples’ mentioned in the beginning of this section.






TipTwo simple examples of limits at infinity




Example 3 Consider the function \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \(f(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{x^{2}+1}\). Whenever \(x\neq 0\), we can write \[
f(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{x^{2}+1}=\frac{x^{2}}{x^{2}(1+\frac{1}{x^{2}})}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{x^{2}}}.
\] Consequently, we have the function \(g\colon (0,+\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \[
g(x)=f(x)=\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{x^{2}}}
\] and Exercise 3 implies \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow+\infty}g(x)=\lim_{x\rightarrow+\infty}f(x).
\tag{5}\] The denominator of \(g\colon (0,+\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) is the sum of the constant function \(h\colon (0,+\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \(h(x)=1\) with the function \(t\colon (0,+\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \(t(x)=\frac{1}{x^{2}}\). Applying the product rule in Proposition 5 to the second example in Example 2 leads to \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow +\infty}t(x)=\lim_{x\rightarrow +\infty} \frac{1}{x^{2}}=0
\] Then, Equation 5 and the quotient rule in Proposition 5 allow us to conclude that \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow +\infty}f(x)=\lim_{x\rightarrow +\infty}g(x)=\lim_{x\rightarrow +\infty} \frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{x^{2}}}=1
\]



Also the squeeze theorem can be adapted to limits at infinity.






NoteThe squeeze (pinching) theorem for limits at infinity




Theorem 2 Let \(\pm\infty\) be an accumulation point of \(D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\), and consider the functions \(f,g\colon D\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\). If \(g(x)\leq f(x)\) for all \(x\in D\) and \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty}g(x)= L,
\] according to Definition 2 or Definition 3, then it follows that \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty}f(x)=L.
\]


Proof:

The proof is similar to that given here, but it will likely take me some time to upload it.




We can also adapt the proposition on the limit of composite functions to the case of unbounded limits.






NoteLimit at infinity of composite functions




Proposition 6 Let \(\pm\infty\) be an accumulation point of \(D'\subseteq \mathbb{R}\), and consider the function \(g\colon D' \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) such that \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty}g(x) = l
\] in the sense of Definition 2 or Definition 3. If \(l\) (which is possibly \(\pm\infty\)) is an accumulation point of \(D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\), and the functions \(f\colon D \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) is such that \[
\lim_{y\rightarrow l} f(y) =L ,
\] according to this definition, or Definition 1, Definition 2, or Definition 3, the equality \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty} f\circ g(x)=L
\] holds if there exists \(M_0>0\) such that for all \(|x|>M_0\), we have \(g(x)\in D\), and:

if \(l\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(L\in\mathbb{R}\), either \(l\in D\) and \(f(l)=L\), or there exists \(M_1>0\) such that for all \(|x|> M_{1}\) it holds \(g(x)\in D -\{l\}\);
if \(l\in\mathbb R\) and \(L=\pm\infty\), there exists \(M_1>0\) such that for all \(|x|> M_{1}\) it holds \(g(x)\in D -\{l\}\);
if \(l=\pm\infty\), there exist \(K,M_{2}>0\) such that for all \(|x|> M_{2}\) it holds \(g(x)\in D\cap\{y\colon |y|> K\}\).

When \(l\in\mathbb{R}\), a similar result holds for left and right limits provided the obvious modifications are implemented.


Proof:

It will take me some time to upload the proof.






4 Discontinuities
Not all functions are continuous, and we now consider the different ways in which a function can fail to be continuous at a point. Consider the function \(f\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\), and let \(x_{0}\) be an accumulation point for \(D\). Three situations are possibles:

removable discontinuity: the limit at \(x_{0}\) exists, but either \(x_{0}\) is not in \(D\), or the limit is different from \(f(x_{0})\);
jump discontinuity: the right and left limits at \(x_{0}\in D\) exist, are finite, but are different;
essential discontinuity: either the left or right limit at \(x_{0}\) does not exist (or, when improper limits are allowed, both limits at \(x_{0}\) exist but at least one of them is either \(+\infty\) or \(-\infty\)).

In the first case (removable discontinuity), we can define a new function \(\tilde{f}\colon D \cup\{x_{0}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) by setting \[
\tilde{f}(x)= \left\{\begin{matrix} f(x) & \mbox{ if } x_{0}\neq x\in D \\  \lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}f(x) & \mbox{ if } x=x_{0} .\end{matrix}\right.
\] This new function is called an extension by continuity of \(f\) and it is a continuous function at \(x_{0}\) by construction. Note that this procedure works whether \(x_{0}\) is in the domain \(D\) of the original function or not. If \(x_{0}\) were in \(D\), then we are redefining \(f\) at that point. If \(x_{0}\) was not in \(D\), then we are genuinely extending \(f\).
In the second case (jump discontinuity), whether \(x_{0}\) lies in \(D\) or not, we can not redefine \(f\) in such a way that the result is a continuous function at \(x_{0}\). The best we can do is obtain an extension of \(f\) which is either left or right continuous at \(x_{0}\).
In the third case (essential singularity), there is nothing we can do to ameliorate the discontinuities of the function \(f\).






CautionExamples of discontinuous functions




Exercise 4 For each type of discontinuity, build a function presenting said discontinuity at least at one point.





5 Exercises






CautionThe square root




Exercise 5 Consider the function \(f\colon (0,+\infty)\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) given by \(f(x)=\sqrt{x}\). Prove that \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow+\infty} \sqrt{x}=+\infty.
\]


Solution:

You are strongly invited to try to solve it on your own.










CautionExercises to keep up in good shape




Exercise 6 All the functions defined by the formulas given below are implicitely assumed to be defined on their maximal domains. Calculate the limits, or prove they do not exist, explaining which previous results you are using in each case: \[
\begin{split}
1) \quad & \lim_{x\rightarrow 1^{\pm}}\, \frac{x^{2}-1}{ x^{2} -2x + 1 }= \pm\infty \\ & \\
2) \quad & \lim_{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}\, \frac{\sqrt{x^{2} -4}}{x-2} = +\infty
\end{split}
\]


Solution:


When \(x=1\), both numerator and denominator vanish, and we get the indeterminate form “\(\frac{0}{0}\)”. The fact that both polynomials have a common root (\(x=1\)) suggests we factorize them. In particular, it holds \[
x^{2}-1=(x-1)(x+1), \quad \mbox{ and }\qquad x^{2}-2x +1=(x-1)(x-1),
\] and thus \[
\frac{x^{2}-1}{x^{2}-2x+1}=\frac{x+1}{x-1}.
\] Now, the numerator tends to 2 when \(x\rightarrow 1^{\pm}\), while the denominator tends to \(0\). Therefore, using Proposition 2, we obtain that the limit is \(+\infty\) when \(x\rightarrow 1^{+}\) (because the denominator tends to \(0\) from the left), and \(-\infty\) when \(x\rightarrow 1^{-}\) (because the denominator tends to \(0\) from the right).
When \(x=2\), both numerator and denominator vanish, and we get the indeterminate form “\(\frac{0}{0}\)”. Putting the denominator in the square root, and using the equality \[
(x^{2} -4)=(x-2)(x+2),
\] we obtain \[
\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}-4}}{x-2}=\sqrt{\frac{x+2}{x-2}}.
\] Then, the rest of the proof uses the limit of composite functions (with the outer function equal to the square root function) and a reasoning analogous to that of the previous point.

title: Sets and functions

1 Introduction


2 Naive set theory
We begin with two primitive informal notions: objects and sets. Roughly speaking, a set is a collection of objects, and the most basic question we can ask is whether a given object belongs to a given set. If the object \(x\) belongs to the set \(A\), we write \[
x\in A,
\] and if it does not belong to \(A\), we write \[
x\notin A.
\]
An intuitive example of set is given by the set of natural numbers \[
\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,3,\dots\},
\] which, at this stage, should be understood only informally.






WarningNumbers will NOT be built




Remark 1. In this course, we will unfortunately not build the set of natural numbers \(\mathbb{N}\), of integers \(\mathbb{Z}\), of rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\), or of real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) from scratch.
Doing so carefully would be supremely satisfying from the intellectual point of view, but it would also require a substantial amount of additional time to go through a similarly substantial amount of foundational material.
In any case, we will explicitly point out the properties and subtleties of these number systems whenever they become relevant.



This informal viewpoint is useful, but also delicate. If one tries to take the notion of set completely literally and declare that every possible collection of objects is automatically a set, contradictions appear. The most famous one is Russell’s paradox, which can be explained through the barber’s paradox: imagine a barber who lives in a village and shaves exactly those people in the village who do not shave themselves. Does the barber shave himself? If he does, then by definition he should not; if he does not, then by definition he should. The set-theoretic Russel’s paradox has the same logical flavour and warns us that foundations must be handled with care. Taking that issue seriously would force us into a long discussion on logic and the foundations of mathematics, which is far beyond the scope of this course. So we adopt a pragmatic axiomatic point of view.
In these notes, we work with objects and sets, and we regard every set as an object. However, not every object is automatically considered to be a set. For instance, the number \(42\) is an object, but Axiom 4 below assures there is set \(\{42\}\) containing the number 42, which is also an object.






NoteAxioms of Set Theory





Sets Are Objects: Every set is an object.
Equality of Sets: Two sets \(A\) and \(B\) are said to be equal if they have exactly the same elements, that is, if for every object \(x\) one has \[
x\in A \Longleftrightarrow x\in B.
\] Thus, when dealing with sets, what matters is not the order in which the elements are written, nor how many times they are listed, but only which objects belong to the set.
Empty Set: There exists a set with no elements, called the empty set and denoted by \[
\emptyset=\{\}.
\]
Singleton sets and pair sets: If \(x\) is an object, then there exists a set whose only element is \(x\). This set is called the singleton associated with \(x\) and is denoted by \[
\{x\}.
\] If \(x\) and \(y\) are objects, then there exists a set whose elements are exactly \(x\) and \(y\). This set is denoted by \[
\{x,y\}.
\] If \(x=y\), this is just the singleton \(\{x\}\).
Pairwise Union: If \(A\) and \(B\) are sets, then there exists a set whose elements are precisely those objects that belong to \(A\) or to \(B\). This set is called the union of \(A\) and \(B\) and is denoted by \[
A\cup B.
\]
Specification: Let \(A\) be a set, and let \(P(x)\) be a property referring to objects \(x\). Then there exists a set consisting of exactly those elements of \(A\) for which \(P(x)\) is true. We denote it by \[
\{x\in A \,:\, P(x)\}.
\] This is the basic operation that allows us to carve out subsets from sets that already exist.
Replacement: Let \(A\) be a set, and suppose that to each element \(x\in A\) we assign a unique object \(f(x)\). Then the collection of all such outputs \[
\{f(x)\,:\, x\in A\}
\] is again a set. This axiom says that if we start with a set and systematically replace each of its elements by another object, the resulting collection is still a set.
Natural Numbers: There exists a set \(\mathbb{N}\) whose elements are called the natural numbers, together with a distinguished element \(0\in\mathbb{N}\) and a successor operation \[
n\mapsto n+1
\] which sends each natural number to another natural number.
Power set:




The previous axioms are enough for the level of set theory we need in this course.






NoteSubset




Definition 1 Given two sets \(A\) and \(X\), we write \[
A\subseteq X
\] if every element of \(A\) is also an element of \(X\). In this case, we call \(A\) a subset of \(X\).
If \(A\neq X\), which means there is at least one element of \(X\) that is not in \(A\), we say \(A\) is a strict subset, and write \(A\subset X\).









NoteIntersection




Definition 2 If \(A\) and \(B\) are subsets of \(X\), we define their intersection is the set \[
A\cap B:=\{x\in A \,:\, x\in B\}.
\]









NoteDifference and complement set




Definition 3 If \(A\) and \(B\) are subsets of \(X\), their difference is the set \[
A\setminus B:=\{x\in A \,:\, x\notin B\}.
\]
In particular, when \(A=X\), the difference \(X\setminus B\) is called the complement of \(B\) in \(X\), and it is often denoted as \(B^{c}\) when \(X\) is understood from the context.









NoteCartesian product




Definition 4 For two sets \(A\) and \(B\), their Cartesian product is the set \[
A\times B:=\{(a,b)\,:\, a\in A,\ b\in B\}.
\] Here \((a,b)\) denotes the ordered pair formed by \(a\) and \(b\).
More generally, if \(A_{1},\dots,A_{n}\) are sets, we define their finite Cartesian product by \[
\prod_{j=1}^{n}A_{j}
:=
\left\{(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\,:\, x_{j}\in A_{j}\ \mbox{ for every } j=1,\dots,n\right\}.
\]









WarningOrdered pairs




Remark 2. In order for Definition 4 to actually make sense, we must be able to consider \((a,b)\) an object, and to be sure that \((a,b)\) is the same object as \((a',b')\) if and only if \(a=a'\) and \(b=b'\).
To do this, we need the so-called Kuratowski’s definition of ordered pairs, which defines \[
(a,b):=\{\{a\},\{a,b\}\}.
\]









NoteRelation on a set




Definition 5 Let \(X\) be a set. A relation on \(X\) is a subset \[
R\subseteq X\times X.
\] If \((x,y)\in R\), we often write \[
x\,R\,y.
\]
Thus, a relation is simply a systematic way of declaring, for some ordered pairs \((x,y)\) of elements of \(X\), that \(x\) is related to \(y\).









NoteOrder relations




Definition 6 Let \(X\) be a set, and let \(\leq\) be a relation on \(X\). We say that \(\leq\) is a partial order if the following properties hold for every \(x,y,z\in X\):

Reflexivity: \(x\leq x\).
Antisymmetry: if \(x\leq y\) and \(y\leq x\), then \(x=y\).
Transitivity: if \(x\leq y\) and \(y\leq z\), then \(x\leq z\).

If, in addition, for every \(x,y\in X\) one has either \(x\leq y\) or \(y\leq x\), then \(\leq\) is called a total order or linear order.
When the order is total, we also write \[
x<y
\] to mean that \(x\leq y\) and \(x\neq y\).









NoteUpper and lower bounds




Definition 7 Let \(X\) be a totally ordered set, and let \(A\subseteq X\).
An element \(u\in X\) is called an upper bound for \(A\) if \[
a\leq u
\] for every \(a\in A\).
An element \(\ell\in X\) is called a lower bound for \(A\) if \[
\ell\leq a
\] for every \(a\in A\).
An upper bound \(s\) for \(A\) is called the least upper bound or supremum of \(A\) if \[
s\leq u
\] for every upper bound \(u\) of \(A\).
A lower bound \(m\) for \(A\) is called the greatest lower bound or infimum of \(A\) if \[
\ell\leq m
\] for every lower bound \(\ell\) of \(A\).
If \(A\) has a least upper bound, we write \[
\sup A.
\] If \(A\) has a greatest lower bound, we write \[
\inf A.
\]
A totally ordered set is said to have the least-upper-bound property if every nonempty subset which is bounded above has a supremum.









NoteField




Definition 8 A field is a set \(F\) endowed with two operations, called addition and multiplication, together with two distinguished elements \(0,1\in F\) with \(0\neq 1\), such that the following hold for every \(x,y,z\in F\):

Associativity of addition and multiplication: \[
(x+y)+z=x+(y+z),\qquad (xy)z=x(yz).
\]
Commutativity of addition and multiplication: \[
x+y=y+x,\qquad xy=yx.
\]
Neutral elements: \[
x+0=x,\qquad x\cdot 1=x.
\]
Additive inverses: for every \(x\in F\), there exists an element \(-x\in F\) such that \[
x+(-x)=0.
\]
Multiplicative inverses: for every \(x\in F\) with \(x\neq 0\), there exists an element \(x^{-1}\in F\) such that \[
x\,x^{-1}=1.
\]
Distributive law: \[
x(y+z)=xy+xz.
\]

These axioms allow us to perform the usual algebraic manipulations with sums, differences, products, and quotients by nonzero elements. The familiar number systems \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(\mathbb{R}\) are examples of fields.









NoteOrdered field




Definition 9 An ordered field is a field \(F\) in the sense of Definition 8, together with a total order \(\leq\) (with associated strict order \(<\)), such that

if \(x<y\), then \[
x+z<y+z
\] for every \(z\in F\);
if \(0<x\) and \(0<y\), then \[
0<xy.
\]

Thus, an ordered field is a field in which the algebraic operations and the order relation are compatible. The rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\) and the real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) are the standard examples.









NoteCharacterization of the real numbers




Theorem 1 There exists, up to order-preserving field isomorphism, only one ordered field with the least-upper-bound property. That ordered field is what mathematicians call the set of real numbers, and it can be proved to “coincide” with the intuitive idea we already have of \(\mathbb{R}\).
We will not prove this theorem here. Instead, we simply accept that the familiar real numbers form an ordered field with the least-upper-bound property and use that fact throughout the course.









NoteThe standard number sets inside \(\mathbb{R}\)




Definition 10 Once \(\mathbb{R}\) is in place, we regard the standard number systems as nested subsets \[
\mathbb{N}\subseteq \mathbb{Z}\subseteq \mathbb{Q}\subseteq \mathbb{R}.
\] Here \(\mathbb{N}\) denotes the natural numbers, \(\mathbb{Z}\) the integers, \(\mathbb{Q}\) the rational numbers, and \(\mathbb{R}\) the real numbers.
We will use these inclusions in the usual informal way and think of the algebraic operations and the order on the smaller number sets as inherited from \(\mathbb{R}\).









NoteInduction principle




Proposition 1 Let \(P(n)\) be a statement depending on a natural number \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). Assume that

\(P(0)\) is true;
whenever \(P(n)\) is true, then \(P(n+1)\) is also true.

Then \(P(n)\) is true for every \(n\in\mathbb{N}\).
This is the principle of mathematical induction. In practice, it allows us to prove infinitely many statements, one for each natural number, by verifying only a base case and one inductive step.





3 Functions
Just as relations are special subsets of Cartesian products, functions may be regarded as special relations in which each input determines exactly one output.






NoteFunctions as relations




Definition 11 Let \(D,X,Y\) be sets with \(D\subseteq X\). A function from \(D\) to \(Y\) is a relation \[
f\subseteq D\times Y
\] such that for every \(x\in D\) there exists a unique \(y\in Y\) with \[
(x,y)\in f.
\]
In this situation, we write \[
f\colon D\subseteq X\rightarrow Y
\] and denote by \(f(x)\) the unique element \(y\in Y\) such that \((x,y)\in f\). The set \(D\) is called the domain of \(f\), while \(Y\) is called the codomain of \(f\).









NoteEquality of functions




Definition 12 Two functions \[
f\colon D\subseteq X\rightarrow Y
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
g\colon E\subseteq X'\rightarrow Y'
\] are said to be equal if \[
D=E,\qquad Y=Y',
\] and \[
f(x)=g(x)
\] for every \(x\in D\).
Thus, the domain and codomain are part of the data of a function. In particular, the same explicit rule applied to different domains defines different functions. For example, the functions \[
f\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\qquad f(x)=x^{2},
\] and \[
g\colon [0,+\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\qquad g(x)=x^{2},
\] are not equal because their domains are different.









NoteComposition of functions




Definition 13 Consider two functions \[
f\colon D\subseteq X\rightarrow Y
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
g\colon E\subseteq Y\rightarrow Z.
\] Assume that \[
f(x)\in E
\] for every \(x\in D\). Then the composition of \(g\) and \(f\) is the function \[
g\circ f\colon D\subseteq X\rightarrow Z
\] defined by \[
(g\circ f)(x):=g(f(x)).
\]









NoteAssociativity of function composition




Proposition 2 Let \[
f\colon D\subseteq X\rightarrow Y,\qquad
g\colon E\subseteq Y\rightarrow Z,\qquad
h\colon F\subseteq Z\rightarrow W
\] be functions such that the compositions involved are well defined. Then \[
h\circ (g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f.
\]


Proof:

Both sides are functions from \(D\) to \(W\). For every \(x\in D\), one has \[
\bigl(h\circ (g\circ f)\bigr)(x)=h\bigl((g\circ f)(x)\bigr)=h(g(f(x))),
\] while \[
\bigl((h\circ g)\circ f\bigr)(x)=(h\circ g)(f(x))=h(g(f(x))).
\] Hence the two functions have the same domain, the same codomain, and the same values on every point of the domain. By Definition 12, they are equal.










WarningHow we will write functions




Remark 3. Sometimes, we may be forced to talk about the function \(f\colon D\subseteq X\rightarrow Y\) given by \(f(x)=y\) multiple times when proving a theorem, solving an exercise, or discussing an idea. To avoid an absurd amount of notationally-heavy repetitions, once the domain, the input space, the output space, and the explicit rule \(f(x)=y\) have been clearly defined as above, we will often write just \(f(x)=y\), or even just \(f\), for the rest of the proof of the theorem, or of the exercise, or of the discussion.
Moreover, sometimes we may be introducing a subset \(D\subseteq X\), and later introduce a function having \(D\) as domain. In this case, we often writes \(f\colon D\rightarrow Y\) given by \(f(x)=y\) omitting the input space since it is clear from the context.









NoteInjective, surjective, and bijective functions




Definition 14 Consider the function \[
f\colon D\subseteq X\rightarrow Y.
\]
We say that \(f\) is injective if \[
f(x)=f(x') \Longrightarrow x=x'
\] for every \(x,x'\in D\).
We say that \(f\) is surjective if for every \(y\in Y\) there exists \(x\in D\) such that \[
f(x)=y.
\]
We say that \(f\) is bijective if it is both injective and surjective.









NoteImage and inverse image




Definition 15 Consider the function \[
f\colon D\subseteq X\rightarrow Y.
\]
If \(A\subseteq D\), the image of \(A\) through \(f\) is the subset of \(Y\) defined by \[
f(A):=\{f(x)\,:\, x\in A\}.
\]
If \(B\subseteq Y\), the inverse image of \(B\) through \(f\) is the subset of \(D\) defined by \[
f^{-1}(B):=\{x\in D \,:\, f(x)\in B\}.
\]
In particular, the image of the whole domain is \[
f(D)=\{f(x)\,:\, x\in D\}\subseteq Y.
\] Thus, the function \(f\) is surjective if and only if \[
f(D)=Y.
\]
Note that the notation \(f^{-1}(B)\) for inverse image makes sense whether or not the function \(f\) admits an inverse function.









NoteLeft inverse, right inverse, and inverse function




Definition 16 Let \[
f\colon D\subseteq X\rightarrow Y.
\] The identity function on \(D\) is the function \[
\mathrm{id}_{D}\colon D\rightarrow D
\] defined by \[
\mathrm{id}_{D}(x)=x.
\]
A function \[
g\colon Y\rightarrow D
\] is called a left inverse of \(f\) if \[
g\circ f=\mathrm{id}_{D}.
\]
A function \[
h\colon Y\rightarrow D
\] is called a right inverse of \(f\) if \[
f\circ h=\mathrm{id}_{Y}.
\]
If a function \(u\colon Y\rightarrow D\) is both a left inverse and a right inverse of \(f\), then \(u\) is called the inverse function of \(f\) and is denoted by \[
f^{-1}\colon Y\rightarrow D.
\] In that case, \[
f^{-1}\circ f=\mathrm{id}_{D}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
f\circ f^{-1}=\mathrm{id}_{Y}.
\]









NoteBasic properties of inverses




Proposition 3 Let \[
f\colon D\subseteq X\rightarrow Y.
\]

If \(f\) admits a left inverse, then \(f\) is injective.
If \(f\) admits a right inverse, then \(f\) is surjective.
If \(f\) admits both a left inverse and a right inverse, then they coincide.
The function \(f\) admits an inverse function if and only if it is bijective.
If the inverse function exists, then it is unique, it is bijective, and \[
\left(f^{-1}\right)^{-1}=f.
\]



Proof:

Suppose first that \(g\colon Y\rightarrow D\) is a left inverse of \(f\). If \(f(x)=f(x')\), then \[
x=(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))=g(f(x'))=(g\circ f)(x')=x',
\] so \(f\) is injective.
Now suppose that \(h\colon Y\rightarrow D\) is a right inverse of \(f\). For every \(y\in Y\), one has \[
f(h(y))=(f\circ h)(y)=y,
\] so every element of \(Y\) belongs to the image of \(f\). Thus \(f\) is surjective.
Assume next that \(g\) is a left inverse and \(h\) is a right inverse of \(f\). Then \[
g=g\circ \mathrm{id}_{Y}=g\circ (f\circ h)=(g\circ f)\circ h=\mathrm{id}_{D}\circ h=h,
\] so they coincide.
If \(f\) admits an inverse function, then it admits both a left inverse and a right inverse, hence by the first two points it is bijective.
Conversely, assume that \(f\) is bijective. Given \(y\in Y\), surjectivity guarantees the existence of \(x\in D\) such that \(f(x)=y\), and injectivity guarantees that this \(x\) is unique. We may therefore define a function \[
f^{-1}\colon Y\rightarrow D
\] by declaring \(f^{-1}(y)\) to be the unique \(x\in D\) such that \(f(x)=y\). By construction, \[
f^{-1}\circ f=\mathrm{id}_{D}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
f\circ f^{-1}=\mathrm{id}_{Y},
\] so \(f^{-1}\) is indeed an inverse function.
Uniqueness follows from point 3: any left inverse and right inverse must coincide. Finally, if \(f^{-1}\) exists, then the identities above show that \(f\) is the inverse of \(f^{-1}\), hence \[
\left(f^{-1}\right)^{-1}=f.
\]






4 Subsets of real numbers
We need to introduce various types of intervals. These objects help in formalizing the way \(x\) approaches \(x_{0}\).






NoteOpen and closed intervals




Definition 17 Let \(a<b\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\cup\{-\infty\}\). Here and throughout, inequalities involving \(\pm\infty\) use the usual order on the extended real line. We define the open interval \((a,b)\) as the subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) given by \[
(a,b):= \{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad a< x < b \}.
\tag{1}\] If either \(a=-\infty\) or \(b=+\infty\), the interval is said to be unbounded.
When \(a\neq-\infty\) and \(b\neq+\infty\), we define the closed interval \([a,b]\) as \[
[a,b]:= \{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad a\leq x \leq b \}.
\]
Intuitively speaking, the interval \((a,b)\) is open because its boundary points are not part of it, while \([a,b]\) is closed because its boundary points are part of it.



Not all intervals are either open or closed. For instance, when \(a\neq-\infty\), we can define the interval \([a,b)\) as \[
[a,b) := \{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad a\leq x < b\},
\] while, when \(b\neq+\infty\), we can define the interval \((a,b]\) as \[
(a,b] := \{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad a < x \leq b\},
\] and it’s clear that these interval are neither open nor closed in the sense of Definition 17
In the following, it will be useful to also consider the symmetric open interval \[
I_{x_{0},\varepsilon}\equiv(x_{0}-\varepsilon, x_{0}+\varepsilon)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad x_{0}-\varepsilon < x < x_{0} + \varepsilon\}
\] centered at \(x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}\) with length \(2\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon>0\). It is not hard to see that if \(x\in I_{x_{0},\varepsilon}\), then either \(x-x_{0}< \varepsilon\) or \(x_{0} - x <\varepsilon\). It then follows that \(|x-x_{0}|<\varepsilon\), so that \[
I_{x_{0},\varepsilon}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\,| \quad d(x_{0},x)<\varepsilon\}.
\] Therefore, the symmetric open intervals of \(\mathbb{R}\) may be determined through the distance function.






NoteAccumulation point




Definition 18 A point \(x_{0}\in \mathbb{R}\) is said to be a left accumulation point for the subset \(D\) if for every \(r>0\) there exists \(x\in D\) such that \[
x_0-r<x<x_0.
\] A point \(x_{0}\in \mathbb{R}\) is said to be a right accumulation point for \(D\) if for every \(r>0\) there exists \(x\in D\) such that \[
x_0<x<x_0+r.
\]
A point which is a left (right) accumulation point but not a right (left) accumulation point is called a strict left accumulation point (strict right accumulation point).
A point \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}\) is said to be an accumulation point for \(D\) if for every \(r>0\) there exists \(x\in D\) with \(x\neq x_0\) such that \[
|x-x_0|<r,
\] which means it is both a left and right accumulation point.









NoteIsolated point




Definition 19 Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) and let \(x_{0}\in D\). We say that \(x_{0}\) is an isolated point of \(D\) if there exists \(r>0\) such that \[
D\cap(x_{0}-r,x_{0}+r)=\{x_{0}\}.
\]









NoteAccumulation at infinity




Definition 20 Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\). We say that \(+\infty\) is a right accumulation point for \(D\) if for every \(R>0\) there exists \(x\in D\) such that \[
x>R.
\] We say that \(-\infty\) is a left accumulation point for \(D\) if for every \(R>0\) there exists \(x\in D\) such that \[
x<-R.
\]

title: Derivatives and differentiability
text:
1 Introduction


2 Derivative and differentiability
Let’s start with the very definition of derivative of a function at a point of its domain.






NoteDerivative and differentiability




Definition 1 Consider the function \(f\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) and a accumulation point \(x_{0}\in D\).
Define the set of admissible increments \[
H_{x_{0}}:=\{h\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\,:\,x_{0}+h\in D\},
\] and the function \(\Delta f\colon H_{x_{0}}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) by \[
\Delta f(h):=\frac{f(x_{0}+h) - f(x_{0})}{h} .
\] Note that \(h=0\) is an accumulation point of \(H_{x_{0}}\).
If the limit \[
\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\Delta f(h)=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x_{0}+h)-f(x_{0})}{h}= l
\] exists with \(l\in\mathbb{R}\), we say that \(l\) is the derivative of \(f\) at \(x_{0}\), that \(f\) is differentiable at \(x_{0}\), and we write \[
f'(x_{0})\equiv \lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\Delta f(h)=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x_{0}+h)-f(x_{0})}{h}=l.
\] We also write \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d} x}(x_{0})\equiv f'(x_{0}),
\] and refer to this expression as the Leibniz notation for derivatives.
If \(f\) is differentiable at all \(x\in D\), we say that \(f\) is differentiable in \(D\).
The function determined by the rule \(x\mapsto f'(x)\) (whenever it makes sense) is called the derivative of \(f\), and its domain need not coincide with the domain of \(f\).



Before we learn some useful tricks that make computing (a lot but not all) derivatives a sort of mechanical task that does not require computing limits, let’s work out some derivatives from the very definition.






TipDerivative of constant functions




Example 1 The first example of derivative we consider is that of a constant function \(f(x)=c\) with \(c\in \mathbb{R}\). Following the very definition of derivative given above, we have \[
f'(x_{0})=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x_{0}+h)-f(x_{0})}{h}=0
\] for every \(x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}\).









TipDerivative of linear functions




Example 2 The second example we consider is that of the linear function \(f(x)=ax\) with \(a\in\mathbb{R}\): \[
f'(x_{0})=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x_{0}+h)-f(x_{0})}{h}=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \frac{a(x_{0} + h) -ax_{0}}{h}=a
\] for every \(x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}\).









TipDerivative of quadratic functions




Example 3 The third example we consider is that of the function \(f(x)=ax^{2}\): \[
\begin{split}
f'(x_{0})&=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x_{0}+h)-f(x_{0})}{h}= \\ &=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \frac{a(x_{0} + h)^{2} -ax_{0}^{2}}{h}= \\ &\lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \frac{2ax_{0}h + ah^{2}}{h}=2ax_{0}
\end{split}
\] for every \(x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}\).



We defined the derivative of \(f\) at \(x_{0}\) assuming \(x_{0}\) is an accumulation point. However, we can also relax this assumption to the case where \(x_{0}\) is either a left or right accumulation point, obtaining the notions of left/right derivative and differentiability.






CautionRight and left derivative




Exercise 1 Consider the function \(f\colon D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\).
If \(x_{0}\in D\) is a left or right accumulation point, define the right or left derivative and differentiability of \(f\) at \(x_{0}\) using left/right limits, and prove that, when \(x_{0}\) is both a left and right accumulation point, the differentiability of \(f\) at \(x_{0}\) is equivalent to left and right differentiability.


Solution:

You are strongly invited to try to solve it on your own.




Just as it happens for limits, derivatives behave well with respect to restrictions.






CautionDerivative of the restriction




Exercise 2 Consider \(D,D'\subseteq \mathbb{R}\) such that \(D\cap D'\neq \emptyset\), and consider two functions \(f\colon D\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) and \(g\colon D' \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) such that both are differentiable at \(x_{0}\in D\cap D'\). Assume there is a subset \(S\subseteq D\cap D'\) such that \(x_{0}\) is an accumulation point for \(S\) and \(g(x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in S\). Prove that \[
f'(x_{0})=g'(x_{0}),
\] and prove analogous results for the case of left and right derivatives.


Solution:

TBA




Once a definition is in place, it’s always a good idea to go searching for situations in which the definition itself can not be applied.






TipAbsolute value function is not differentiable at \(x=0\)




Example 4 Let us consider the absolute value function \(|\cdot|\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \[
|x|=\sqrt{x^{2}}=\left\{\begin{matrix}x & \mbox{ if } x\geq 0 \\ & \\ -x & \mbox{ if } x<0 .\end{matrix}\right.
\] For all points \(x_{0}\neq 0\), we can compute the derivative following Example 2 (essentially because of Exercise 2). However, when \(x_{0}=0\), we have to take into account the “sudden change” of the function. Therefore, we first compute the right and left derivatives: \[
\begin{split}
\lim_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{x-0}{x}&=1 \\ & \\
\lim_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}\frac{-x-0}{x}&=-1 .
\end{split}
\] Since the two derivatives exist but are different, we conclude that \(|x|\) is not differentiable at \(0\) (but it is separately left and right differentiable there).





3 Properties of derivatives
The first “property” of derivatives we want to highlight is that it requires continuity.






NoteDifferentiability implies continuity




Proposition 1 If the function \(f\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) is (left/right) differentiable at \(x_{0}\in D\), then it is also (left/right) continuous at \(x_{0}\).


Proof:

You are strongly invited to try to prove it on your own.




Note, however, that the converse of the previous proposition does not hold. An explicit counterexample is given by the absolute value function in Example 4.
Next, we pass to how derivatives behave with respect to sums and products of 2 functions.






NoteAlgebraic manipulations of derivatives




Proposition 2 Given \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\) and the functions \(f,g\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) differentiable at \(x_{0}\in D\), the functions \(h,r\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \(h:=\alpha f+\beta g\) and \(r:=f\cdot g\) are differentiable at \(x_{0}\) and their derivatives are \[
\begin{split}
h'(x_{0})&=\alpha f'(x_{0}) + \beta g'(x_{0}),\\
r'(x_{0})& =f'(x_{0})\,g(x_{0}) + f(x_{0})\,g'(x_{0}).
\end{split}
\] The formula for the derivative of the product of two functions is usually referred to as the Leibniz rule.


Proof:

TBA




What happens when we have more than 2 functions? For a small number of functions, say between 3 and 7, it should be not extremely boring to use the associativity property of function sums and products to understand how to generalize Proposition 2. For an arbitrary finite number of functions, the generalization can be obtained using the induction principle.






CautionAlgebraic manipulations of derivatives continued




Exercise 3 Let \((\alpha_{1},\cdots\alpha_{n})\) be a finite sequence of real numbers and \((f_{1},\cdots,f_{n})\) a finite sequence of scalar functions with common domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\). Suppose that, at \(x_{0}\in D\), the derivatives \(f_{j}'(x_{0})\) exist for every \(j=1,...,n\). Then, it holds \[
\begin{split}
\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\,\alpha_{j}\,f_{j}\right)'(x_{0}) &=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\, \alpha_{j}\,f_{j}'(x_{0})  \\
\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n} \,\alpha_{j}\,f_{j}\right)'(x_{0}) &=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\,\alpha_{j}\,f_{j}'(x_{0})\,\left(\prod_{k\neq j}\alpha_{k}\,f_{k}(x_{0})\right).
\end{split}
\]


Solution:

Fix an accumulation point \(x_0\in D\) and assume that \(f_j'(x_0)\) exists for all \(j=1,\dots,n\). Set \(g_j:=\alpha_j f_j\), so that \(g_j'(x_0)=\alpha_j f_j'(x_0)\).
We will use the two-function rules from Proposition 2

We start with the derivative of the sum of finitely many functions.
For \(h\neq 0\) with \(x_0+h\in D\), we have \[
\frac{\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j(x_0+h)-\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j(x_0)}{h}
=\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \frac{f_j(x_0+h)-f_j(x_0)}{h}.
\] Following Definition 1, we take the limit as \(h\to 0\): \[
\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\,\alpha_{j}\,f_{j}\right)'(x_{0})
=\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f_j(x_0+h)-f_j(x_0)}{h}
=\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j'(x_0),
\] where we passed the limit through the sum because it’s a sum of finitely many elements.

Now, we pass to the derivative of the product of finitely many functions.
Define \[
P_n(x):=\prod_{j=1}^n g_j(x).
\]
Base case (\(n=1\)): \(P_1=g_1\), hence \[
P_1'(x_0)=g_1'(x_0)
=\sum_{j=1}^1 g_j'(x_0)\prod_{k\neq j} g_k(x_0),
\] so the formula holds.
Inductive step: assume that for some \(n\ge 1\), \[
P_n'(x_0)=\sum_{j=1}^n g_j'(x_0)\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\neq j}}^n g_k(x_0).
\] Now \(P_{n+1}=P_n\,g_{n+1}\). By the two-function product rule, \[
P_{n+1}'(x_0)=P_n'(x_0)\,g_{n+1}(x_0)+P_n(x_0)\,g_{n+1}'(x_0).
\] Substitute the inductive hypothesis into the first term: \[
\begin{aligned}
P_{n+1}'(x_0)
&=\left(\sum_{j=1}^n g_j'(x_0)\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\neq j}}^n g_k(x_0)\right) g_{n+1}(x_0)
+ \left(\prod_{k=1}^n g_k(x_0)\right) g_{n+1}'(x_0)\\[4pt]
&=\sum_{j=1}^n g_j'(x_0)\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\neq j}}^{n+1} g_k(x_0)
\;+\; g_{n+1}'(x_0)\prod_{k=1}^n g_k(x_0)\\[4pt]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{n+1} g_j'(x_0)\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\neq j}}^{n+1} g_k(x_0).
\end{aligned}
\] Finally, replacing \(g_j=\alpha_j f_j\) and \(g_j'(x_0)=\alpha_j f_j'(x_0)\), we obtain \[
\left(\prod_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j\right)'(x_0)
=\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j'(x_0)\left(\prod_{k\neq j}\alpha_k f_k(x_0)\right).
\]
This concludes the proof.










CautionA foundational example




Exercise 4 Let \(n\in \mathbb{N}\). Prove that the derivative of the function \(f_{n}\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \(f_{n}(x)=\alpha_{n}x^{n}\) with \(\alpha_{n}\in \mathbb{R}\) is \(n\alpha_{n}x^{n-1}\).


Solution:

Use Example 2 together with Exercise 3.




Now, we consider what happens to the derivative of the quotient of two functions.






NoteDerivative of the quotient




Proposition 3 Given the functions \(f,g\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) differentiable at \(x_{0}\in D\) and with \(g(x_{0})\neq 0\), define \[
\tilde{D}:=\{x\in D \,:\, g(x)\neq 0\},
\] and the function \(h\colon \tilde{D}\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \(h:=\frac{f}{g}\). Then \(h\) is differentiable at \(x_{0}\) and its derivative is \[
h'(x_{0})= \frac{f'(x_{0})\,g(x_{0})-f(x_{0})\,g'(x_{0})}{(g(x_{0}))^{2}}.
\]


Proof:

TBA




Finally, we are able to use all the results presented in this section to compute the derivatives of polynomial and rational functions without ever computing a limit.






CautionDerivatives of polynomials and rational functions




Exercise 5 Let \(P_{n},Q_{m}\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be polynomial functions. Compute \(P_{n}',Q_{m}'\), and \(R'\), where \(R=\frac{P_{n}}{Q_{m}}\) is defined on the maximal domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) on which \(Q_{m}(x)\neq 0\).


Solution:

To compute the derivative of \(P_{n}\), we first write \[
P_{n}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\alpha_{k}\,x^{k}
\] with \(\alpha_{k}\in\mathbb{R}\), and then use Exercise 3 together with Exercise 4 to conclude that the derivative \(P_{n}'\) of \(P_{n}\) is the polynomial of order \((n-1)\) given by \[
P_{n}'(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\alpha_{k}\,x^{k-1}.
\] A similar result holds for \(Q_{m}'(x)\).
The derivative of \(R(x)=\frac{P_{n}(x)}{Q_{m}(x)}\) can then be immediately obtained using the previous results and Proposition 3:
\[
R'(x)=\frac{P'_{n}(x)Q_{m}(x) - P_{n}(x)Q'_{m}(x)}{(Q_{m}(x))^{2}}.
\]






4 Derivative of inverse and composite functions
We previously saw that continuity behaves well under composition of continuous functions and inversion of functions on intervals.
Can we hope for analogous behaviours for differentiable functions? The answer is yes, under suitable hypotheses.






NoteDerivative of composite functions - The chain rule




Proposition 4 Consider the functions \(f\colon D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) and \(g\colon D'\subseteq \mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\), and assume that \(g(D')\subseteq D\). If \(g\) is differentiable at \(x_{0}\in D'\) and \(f\) is differentiable at \(g(x_{0})\in D\), then the composite function \(r:=f\circ g\) is differentiable at \(x_{0}\) and \[
r'(x_{0})=(f\circ g)'(x_{0})=f'(g(x_{0}))\,g'(x_{0}).
\]


Proof:

Define the auxiliary function \(\phi\colon D\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) by \[
\phi(y):=
\left\{
\begin{matrix}
\dfrac{f(y)-f(g(x_{0}))}{y-g(x_{0})} & \mbox{ if } y\neq g(x_{0}), \\ & \\
f'(g(x_{0})) & \mbox{ if } y=g(x_{0}) .
\end{matrix}
\right.
\] Since \(f\) is differentiable at \(g(x_{0})\), it follows from Definition 1 that \[
\lim_{y\rightarrow g(x_{0})}\phi(y)=f'(g(x_{0})),
\] so \(\phi\) is continuous at \(g(x_{0})\).
Moreover, Proposition 1 implies that \(g\) is continuous at \(x_{0}\), that is, \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}g(x)=g(x_{0}).
\] Since \(\phi\) is continuous at \(g(x_{0})\), limit of composite functions implies that \[
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}} \phi(g(x))=\phi(g(x_{0}))=f'(g(x_{0})).
\]
For every \(h\neq 0\) such that \(x_{0}+h\in D'\), we have \[
\frac{r(x_{0}+h)-r(x_{0})}{h}
=\frac{f(g(x_{0}+h))-f(g(x_{0}))}{h}
=\phi(g(x_{0}+h))\,\frac{g(x_{0}+h)-g(x_{0})}{h}.
\] Indeed, if \(g(x_{0}+h)\neq g(x_{0})\), the identity follows from the definition of \(\phi\), while if \(g(x_{0}+h)= g(x_{0})\), both sides are equal to \(0\).
Passing to the limit as \(h\to 0\), we obtain \[
\begin{split}
r'(x_{0})
&=\lim_{h\to 0}\phi(g(x_{0}+h))\,\frac{g(x_{0}+h)-g(x_{0})}{h} \\
&=\left(\lim_{h\to 0}\phi(g(x_{0}+h))\right)\left(\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{g(x_{0}+h)-g(x_{0})}{h}\right) \\
&=f'(g(x_{0}))\,g'(x_{0}),
\end{split}
\] as claimed.










CautionA first exercise on the chain rule




Exercise 6 Compute the derivative of the function \(f\colon\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \[
f(x)=\left(x^{2}+1\right)^{3}.
\]


Solution:

Define \[
g(x):=x^{2}+1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
h(y):=y^{3},
\] so that \(f=h\circ g\).
From Example 3, Example 1, and Proposition 2, we obtain \[
g'(x)=2x.
\] From Exercise 4, we know that \[
h'(y)=3y^{2}.
\] Applying Proposition 4, we conclude that \[
f'(x)=h'(g(x))\,g'(x)=3(x^{2}+1)^{2}\cdot 2x=6x(x^{2}+1)^{2}.
\]










NoteDerivative of inverse functions




Proposition 5 Let \(I\) be an interval, let \(f\colon I\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be differentiable and invertible on \(I\), and set \(J:=f(I)\). Fix \(x_{0}\in I\) and write \(y_{0}:=f(x_{0})\). If \(f'(x_{0})\neq 0\), then the inverse function \(f^{-1}\colon J\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) is differentiable at \(y_{0}\) and \[
\left(f^{-1}\right)'(y_{0})=\frac{1}{f'(x_{0})}.
\]


Proof:

Since \(f\) is differentiable on \(I\), Proposition 1 implies that \(f\) is continuous on \(I\). Therefore, continuity of inverse function guarantees that \(f^{-1}\) is continuous on \(J\).
Take \(y\in J\) with \(y\neq y_{0}\), and set \(x:=f^{-1}(y)\). Then \(x\neq x_{0}\) because \(f\) is invertible, and \(y=f(x)\). Hence \[
\frac{f^{-1}(y)-f^{-1}(y_{0})}{y-y_{0}}
=\frac{x-x_{0}}{f(x)-f(x_{0})}
=\left(\frac{f(x)-f(x_{0})}{x-x_{0}}\right)^{-1}.
\]
Now let \(y\rightarrow y_{0}\) in \(J\). Since \(f^{-1}\) is continuous at \(y_{0}\) by continuity of inverse function, we have \[
x=f^{-1}(y)\rightarrow f^{-1}(y_{0})=x_{0}.
\] Therefore, \[
\begin{split}
\left(f^{-1}\right)'(y_{0})
&=\lim_{y\rightarrow y_{0}}\frac{f^{-1}(y)-f^{-1}(y_{0})}{y-y_{0}} \\
&=\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}\left(\frac{f(x)-f(x_{0})}{x-x_{0}}\right)^{-1} \\
&=\left(\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}\frac{f(x)-f(x_{0})}{x-x_{0}}\right)^{-1} \\
&=\frac{1}{f'(x_{0})},
\end{split}
\] where the reciprocal is legitimate because \(f'(x_{0})\neq 0\).










CautionDerivative of root functions




Exercise 7 Let \(n\in \mathbb{N}\) with \(n\geq 1\), and let \(D\) be the maximal domain on which the function \[
p_{n}(x)=x^{n}
\] admits an inverse denoted by \(g\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) and given by \(g(y)=y^{\frac{1}{n}}\). Explicitly, \(D=\mathbb{R}\) if \(n\) is odd and \(D=\mathbb{R}_{+}=(0,\infty)\) if \(n\) is even.
Use Proposition 5 to compute the derivative of \(g\) at points \(y_{0}\in p_{n}(D)\) for which the proposition applies.


Solution:

Fix \(y_{0}\in p_{n}(D)\) and set \(x_{0}:=g(y_{0})=y_{0}^{\frac{1}{n}}\). By Exercise 4, the derivative of \(p_{n}\) is \[
p_{n}'(x)=nx^{n-1}.
\] Therefore, if \(x_{0}\neq 0\), then \[
p_{n}'(x_{0})=n x_{0}^{n-1}\neq 0,
\] and Proposition 5 yields \[
g'(y_{0})=\frac{1}{p_{n}'(x_{0})}
=\frac{1}{n x_{0}^{n-1}}
=\frac{1}{n\left(y_{0}^{\frac{1}{n}}\right)^{n-1}}
=\frac{1}{n}y_{0}^{\frac{1}{n}-1}.
\]
If \(n>1\) and \(y_{0}=0\), then \(x_{0}=0\) and \[
p_{n}'(0)=0,
\] so Proposition 5 does not apply. Therefore, for \(n>1\), the derivative formula above is valid only at points \(y_{0}\neq 0\).










CautionRight derivative at the origin for even roots




Exercise 8 Let \(\mathbb{N}\ni n\geq 2\) be even. Consider the function \(g\colon \mathbb{R}_{+}\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) given by \[
g(y)=y^{\frac{1}{n}}.
\] Study the right derivative of \(g\) at \(0\).


Solution:

Since \(g(0)=0\), for every \(h>0\) we have \[
\frac{g(0+h)-g(0)}{h}
=\frac{h^{\frac{1}{n}}}{h}
=h^{\frac{1}{n}-1}
=h^{-\frac{n-1}{n}}.
\] Because \(-\frac{n-1}{n}<0\), the previous quantity tends to \(+\infty\) as \(h\rightarrow 0^{+}\).
Therefore, \(g\) does not admit a finite right derivative at \(0\). Equivalently, the right difference quotient has unbounded limit \(+\infty\) at the origin.






5 Interpretation of derivative
From a geometrical point of view, the derivative \(f'(x_{0})\) is related with to slope of the line tangent to the graph of \(f\) at the point \((x_{0},f(x_{0}))\).
Intuitively speaking, the line tangent to the graph of a function at a point is the limit of the secant lines connecting said point with other points on the graph. The following applet allows us to visualize how the secant line approaches the tangent line.




Interactive demo: tangent line intuition (source: https://www.geogebra.org/m/n8ztr6qs).


The intuitive idea of derivative as rate of change often presented may be easy to grasp because it relies on the idea of velocity which the vast majority of humans can understand (even if only in a non-rigorous way). However, this interpretation is not very helpful when the input of the functions considered is no longer a single number (which can always be thought of as being the “time parameter” labeling something that changes).
A perspective which is suitable to multivariable functions is that of thinking of the derivative \(f'(x_{0})\) as providing the best linear approximation of the function near \(x_{0}\). Specifically, we can define \(f'(x_{0})\) as the number (if it exists) such that \[ \lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}\frac{\mid f(x) - [f(x_{0}) +f'(x_{0})\,(x-x_{0})]\mid}{\mid x-x_{0}\mid}=0. \] Roughly speaking, the previous limit is telling us that the difference between \(f(x)\) and \([f(x_{0}) +f'(x_{0})\,(x-x_{0})]\) gets smaller as \(x\) approaches \(x_{0}\), and it gets smaller “faster” than how \(x\) approaches \(x_{0}\) (because the limit with \(x-x_{0}\) in the denominator is zero).
Consequently, when the derivative at \(x_{0}\) exists, we may approximate reasonably well \(f(x)\) with the linear function \([f(x_{0}) + f'(x_{0})\,(x-x_{0})]\) as long as \(x\) is close to \(x_{0}\).


6 Higher order derivatives, \(C^{k}\)-functions, and smooth functions
It may happen that the derivative of a differentiable function is itself differentiable, and that the same phenomenon can be repeated many times. This leads to the notion of higher order derivatives and, later on, to a useful regularity classification of functions.






NoteHigher order derivatives




Definition 2 Consider the function \(f\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\).
If the derivative function \(f'\) is differentiable at \(x_{0}\in D\), then its derivative at \(x_{0}\) is called the second derivative of \(f\) at \(x_{0}\), and is denoted by \[
f''(x_{0})=(f')'(x_{0}).
\] If the derivative of \(f'\) is again differentiable at \(x_{0}\), then we define the third derivative of \(f\) at \(x_{0}\) by \[
f'''(x_{0})=(f'')'(x_{0}),
\] and so on.
More generally, define recursively \[
f^{(0)}:=f.
\] For \(k\in \mathbb{N}\), if \(f^{(k-1)}\) is differentiable at \(x_{0}\), then the derivative of \(f^{(k-1)}\) at \(x_{0}\) is called the \(k\)-th derivative of \(f\) at \(x_{0}\), and is denoted by \[
f^{(k)}(x_{0})=\left(f^{(k-1)}\right)'(x_{0}).
\] We also write \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}^{k}f}{\mathrm{d} x^{k}}(x_{0})\equiv f^{(k)}(x_{0}).
\]
If \(f^{(k)}(x)\) exists for every \(x\in D\), we say that \(f\) is \(k\) times differentiable in \(D\). As for the first derivative, the domain of \(f^{(k)}\) need not coincide with the domain of \(f\).









Note\(C^{k}\)-functions and smooth functions




Definition 3 Let \(k\in \mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}\). We say that the function \(f\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) is of class \(C^{k}\) in \(D\) if, for every \(j=0,\dots,k\), the derivative \(f^{(j)}\) exists in \(D\) and is continuous in \(D\). Here, by convention, \(f^{(0)}=f\), so being of class \(C^{0}\) simply means being continuous.
If \(f\) is of class \(C^{k}\) for every \(k\in \mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}\), then \(f\) is called a smooth function, or a \(C^{\infty}\)-function.
Clearly, if \(f\) is of class \(C^{k}\) with \(k\geq 1\), then it is also of class \(C^{k-1}\).









CautionHigher derivatives of monomials




Exercise 9 Let \(n\in \mathbb{N}\) and \(\alpha_{n}\in\mathbb{R}\). Consider the function \(f_{n}\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) given by \[
f_{n}(x)=\alpha_{n}x^{n}.
\] Compute its \(k\)-th derivative for every \(k\in\mathbb{N}\).


Solution:

From Exercise 4, we know that \[
f_{n}'(x)=n\alpha_{n}x^{n-1}.
\] Applying the same result repeatedly, we obtain \[
\begin{split}
f_{n}''(x)&=n(n-1)\alpha_{n}x^{n-2}, \\
f_{n}'''(x)&=n(n-1)(n-2)\alpha_{n}x^{n-3},
\end{split}
\] and, in general, \[
f_{n}^{(k)}(x)=n(n-1)\cdots (n-k+1)\,\alpha_{n}\,x^{n-k}
=\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\,\alpha_{n}\,x^{n-k}
\] for every \(k=1,\dots,n\).
For \(k=n\), this gives \[
f_{n}^{(n)}(x)=n!\,\alpha_{n},
\] which is a constant function. Therefore, by Example 1, \[
f_{n}^{(n+1)}(x)=0.
\] Applying again Example 1, we conclude that \[
f_{n}^{(k)}(x)=0
\] for every \(k\geq n+1\).










NotePolynomials are smooth




Proposition 6 Every polynomial function \(P\colon\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) is smooth.


Proof:

Write \[
P(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\alpha_{j}x^{j}.
\] Fix \(k\in\mathbb{N}\). By Exercise 9, for every \(j=0,\dots,n\), the \(k\)-th derivative of the monomial \(x\mapsto \alpha_{j}x^{j}\) exists on \(\mathbb{R}\) and is either a monomial or the zero function. In particular, it is continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\).
Using Exercise 3 repeatedly, we conclude that \(P^{(k)}\) exists on \(\mathbb{R}\) and is continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\). Since \(k\) is arbitrary, \(P\) is of class \(C^{k}\) for every \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), hence it is smooth.

3.1 1) Derivative of a finite sum
Define \[
S_n(x):=\sum_{j=1}^n g_j(x).
\]
Base case (\(n=1\)): \(S_1=g_1\), hence \[
S_1'(x_0)=g_1'(x_0)=\alpha_1 f_1'(x_0).
\]
Inductive step: assume the formula holds for \(n\), i.e. \[
S_n'(x_0)=\sum_{j=1}^n g_j'(x_0).
\] Consider \(S_{n+1}=S_n+g_{n+1}\). By the two-function sum rule, \[
S_{n+1}'(x_0)=S_n'(x_0)+g_{n+1}'(x_0)
=\sum_{j=1}^n g_j'(x_0)+g_{n+1}'(x_0)
=\sum_{j=1}^{n+1} g_j'(x_0).
\] Replacing \(g_j'(x_0)\) with \(\alpha_j f_j'(x_0)\) gives \[
\left(\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j\right)'(x_0)=\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j'(x_0).
\]

title: Derivatives and differentiability
text:
3.2 2) Derivative of a finite product
Define \[
P_n(x):=\prod_{j=1}^n g_j(x).
\]
Base case (\(n=1\)): \(P_1=g_1\), hence \[
P_1'(x_0)=g_1'(x_0)
=\sum_{j=1}^1 g_j'(x_0)\prod_{k\neq j} g_k(x_0),
\] so the formula holds.
Inductive step: assume that for some \(n\ge 1\), \[
P_n'(x_0)=\sum_{j=1}^n g_j'(x_0)\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\neq j}}^n g_k(x_0).
\] Now \(P_{n+1}=P_n\,g_{n+1}\). By the two-function product rule, \[
P_{n+1}'(x_0)=P_n'(x_0)\,g_{n+1}(x_0)+P_n(x_0)\,g_{n+1}'(x_0).
\] Substitute the inductive hypothesis into the first term: \[
\begin{aligned}
P_{n+1}'(x_0)
&=\left(\sum_{j=1}^n g_j'(x_0)\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\neq j}}^n g_k(x_0)\right) g_{n+1}(x_0)
+ \left(\prod_{k=1}^n g_k(x_0)\right) g_{n+1}'(x_0)\\[4pt]
&=\sum_{j=1}^n g_j'(x_0)\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\neq j}}^{n+1} g_k(x_0)
\;+\; g_{n+1}'(x_0)\prod_{k=1}^n g_k(x_0)\\[4pt]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{n+1} g_j'(x_0)\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\neq j}}^{n+1} g_k(x_0).
\end{aligned}
\] Finally, replacing \(g_j=\alpha_j f_j\) and \(g_j'(x_0)=\alpha_j f_j'(x_0)\), we obtain \[
\left(\prod_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j\right)'(x_0)
=\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j'(x_0)\left(\prod_{k\neq j}\alpha_k f_k(x_0)\right).
\]
This concludes the proof.
